title: ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE
body:
The course about building things that decide. Its organising idea is the [[Rational Agent]]:
something that perceives an environment and picks the action expected to do best by a performance
measure someone wrote down. Every block is a different answer to *how* it picks, and the blocks
are ordered by how much the agent is told in advance. Search knows the rules and works out the
consequences. Utility theory adds probabilities to consequences it cannot be sure of. Learning
covers the case where nobody supplied the rules, and reinforcement learning the case where nobody
supplied the answers either.

It sits next to [[MACHINE LEARNING]] and the two do not compete. **That course owns learning from
data as a subject in its own right**, the neural-network stack and the loss and evaluation
machinery; **this one owns the agent**, and treats learning as one of several things an agent can
do. The learning blocks below link across rather than restating, and the notes that live here are
the ones that course logged as gaps.

## Topics

### Classical search

[[Best-First Search]] · [[A* Search]] · [[Heuristic]] · [[Heap]] · [[Weighted Graph]] ·
[[Time Complexity]]

[[Best-First Search]] is a family rather than an algorithm: keep the frontier in a priority queue
ordered by an evaluation function $f(n)$, and change $f$ to change what you have. $f = g$ is
Dijkstra, $f = h$ is greedy and not optimal, $f = g + h$ is [[A* Search]].

[[A* Search]] is the one that matters. Because $f$ estimates the cost of the whole solution
*through* a node rather than just the distance left, it stays optimal whenever the
[[Heuristic]] never overestimates, and it degrades to Dijkstra when $h = 0$. **The algorithm is
fixed and the heuristic is the design work**, which is why [[Heuristic]] carries the admissible
and consistent definitions, the dominance rule, and relax-the-problem as the method for inventing
one.

### Adversarial search

[[Game Trees]] · [[Nondeterminism]] · [[NP-Complete]]

**Owned by [[Game Trees]] in [[THE NEW TURING OMNIBUS]] and not restated here.** That note has
minimax, the $O(b^d)$ explosion that makes exhaustive play impossible past checkers, alpha-beta
pruning down to $O(b^{d/2})$ with good move ordering, static evaluation functions, and the horizon
effect. It also carries the Deep-Blue-to-AlphaGo line, which is the shortest route from this block
to the learning ones.

The link back to [[Expected Utility]] is worth noticing: minimax assumes the *worst* case because
the uncertainty is an opponent, while utility theory takes the *expected* case because the
uncertainty is a die. Games with chance need both.

### Optimisation without gradients

[[Genetic Algorithm]] · [[Optimization]] · [[Gradient Descent]] · [[Multivariable Optimization]]

[[Genetic Algorithm]] is population, fitness, selection, crossover, mutation. Crossover is what
makes it evolutionary rather than parallel random restarts; mutation is what escapes local optima.

It earns its place by contrast with [[Gradient Descent]]: gradients need a differentiable
landscape and find a local minimum from a single point, a GA needs only a fitness number and can
work on discrete or black-box problems where "nudge the parameters" means nothing. Neither
dominates, and knowing which shape of problem you have is the actual skill.

### Rational decisions under uncertainty

[[Rational Agent]] · [[Utility Function]] · [[Expected Utility]] · [[Probability]] ·
[[Random Variable]] · [[Bayes Theorem]] · [[Conditional Probability]]

[[Rational Agent]] holds the frame: performance measure, environment, actuators, sensors, plus
the environment properties (observable, deterministic, single-agent, episodic, static, discrete)
that decide which algorithm is even applicable. **Each later block is one of those properties
being relaxed**, which is the best way to remember what each is for.

[[Utility Function]] is why a preference ordering is not enough: ranking outcomes cannot answer
"is a 50% chance of $A$ better than $B$ for certain", because that needs a *how much*. Utility is
concave in money, and that concavity **is** risk aversion, with no extra mechanism.
[[Expected Utility]] is the rule itself, $\sum P(s)U(s)$, maximised. It is an expectation from
[[STATISTICS]] with utilities in place of values, and it justifies risk aversion, the value of
information, and exploration in one go.

### Learning from labels

[[Supervised Learning]] · [[Decision Tree]] · [[Random Forest]] · [[Linear Regression]] ·
[[Logistic Regression]] · [[Gradient Descent]] · [[Loss Function]] · [[Classification]] ·
[[Confusion Matrix]] · [[Sigmoid]]

[[Supervised Learning]] is the frame: labelled examples, regression when the target is a number
and classification when it is a category, and the same four-step loop underneath every model
(choose a model, choose a loss, minimise it, then check on data it has never seen).

The regression and gradient material is already written and lives elsewhere:
[[Linear Regression]] in [[STATISTICS]], [[Logistic Regression]] and [[Gradient Descent]] in
[[THE NEW TURING OMNIBUS]], the evaluation set in [[MACHINE LEARNING]]. What this course adds is
trees. [[Decision Tree]] is **the one model you can read**, and it splits on information gain,
which is [[Entropy]] doing applied work for the first time in the vault. Its defining weakness is
overfitting: grown to full depth it memorises. [[Random Forest]] is the fix that turns the
weakness into the mechanism, since bagging and feature subsampling force the trees to disagree and
uncorrelated errors cancel when averaged.

### Learning without labels

[[Unsupervised Learning]] · [[Clustering]] · [[Principal Component Analysis]] · [[Vector Norm]] ·
[[Mean]] · [[Variance]]

No labels means no right answer and therefore **no way to score the result**, which is the real
difficulty rather than the algorithms. [[Unsupervised Learning]] covers that plus anomaly
detection, where the classes are wildly imbalanced by definition and accuracy is meaningless.

[[Clustering]] rests entirely on what "close" means: distance is a [[Vector Norm]], so feature
scaling changes the answer completely and high dimensions dilute distance until nearest means
nothing. k-means converges to a *local* optimum, assumes spherical clusters of similar size, and
requires you to know $k$, which is the thing you usually wanted to find out.

### Reinforcement learning

[[Reinforcement Learning]] · [[Q-Learning]] · [[Expected Utility]] · [[Neural Network]]

The agent gets neither labels nor structure, only a scalar reward that may arrive long after the
action that earned it. That gap is the **credit assignment problem** and it is what makes this its
own field. [[Reinforcement Learning]] covers the loop, return and discounting, value functions as
[[Expected Utility]] with the utilities unknown, passive against active, and the
exploration/exploitation trade.

[[Q-Learning]] is the algorithm: a table $Q(s,a)$ updated by the temporal-difference error, so it
is **model-free** (never learns how the world works) and **off-policy** (learns the optimal policy
while behaving by another one, which is what lets it explore safely). It converges given enough
visits, and the table is impossible for any real state space, which is where a
[[Neural Network]] replaces it and this course's blocks 3 and 5 meet.

## Core Facts to Know

- A rational agent maximises **expected** performance given what it knows, not actual outcomes.
- Rational is not omniscient; a good decision can have a bad result.
- The performance measure is written by the designer, and writing it badly is the classic failure.
- Best-first search = priority queue ordered by $f(n)$; the algorithm is whichever $f$ you pick.
- $f = g$ is Dijkstra, $f = h$ is greedy best-first (fast, not optimal), $f = g + h$ is $A^*$.
- **Admissible** = never overestimates. **Consistent** = obeys the triangle inequality, and it
  implies admissible.
- $A^*$ is optimal with an admissible $h$, and expands each node once with a consistent one.
- Design a heuristic by solving a relaxed version of the problem exactly.
- If $h_2 \ge h_1$ and both are admissible, $h_2$ dominates and expands fewer nodes.
- $A^*$'s binding constraint is usually memory, not time.
- Minimax assumes an optimal opponent; alpha-beta gives the **same answer** faster.
- A genetic algorithm needs a fitness number, not a derivative, and escapes local optima by
  mutation.
- A preference ordering cannot price uncertainty; utilities can, which is why they are numbers.
- Utility scale is arbitrary: $U$ and $2U + 7$ are the same agent.
- Concave utility in money **is** risk aversion; no extra rule is needed.
- MEU: choose the action maximising $\sum_s P(s \mid a) U(s)$.
- Information is worth exactly what it changes about your decision, and nothing otherwise.
- Supervised = labelled, unsupervised = structure, reinforcement = delayed scalar reward.
- Decision trees split to maximise information gain, which is the [[Entropy]] drop across a split.
- A fully grown tree memorises the training data; that is overfitting, not learning.
- Random forests work because bagging and feature subsampling make errors **uncorrelated**, and
  averaging cancels uncorrelated errors.
- The forest's cost is interpretability, which was the single tree's whole advantage.
- Clustering results depend on feature scaling, so standardise before you cluster.
- k-means converges, but to a local optimum, and it assumes roughly spherical similar-sized
  clusters.
- Choosing $k$ has no correct answer; the elbow and silhouette methods are heuristics.
- Unsupervised learning has no ground truth, so it has no honest accuracy score.
- RL's hard part is **credit assignment**: which of forty moves earned the win.
- The discount factor $\gamma$ is how much the agent cares about the future.
- Q-learning is model-free and off-policy, so it can explore and still learn the optimal policy.
- $\epsilon$-greedy exploration is the value-of-information argument, not a hack.
- A $Q$ table is impossible past toy state spaces; approximating it with a network is deep RL.
- Reward functions, fitness functions, and performance measures are the same failure mode three
  times: the system optimises what you wrote, not what you meant.

## Related courses

- [[MACHINE LEARNING]] is the sibling course and the division is deliberate: it owns learning from
  data as a subject ([[Neural Network]], [[Back Propagation]], [[CNN]], [[Loss Function]],
  [[Confusion Matrix]]), this one owns the agent that might use it. [[Classification]], [[MNIST]],
  and [[Entropy]] are shared.
- [[THE NEW TURING OMNIBUS]]: [[Game Trees]] is this course's adversarial-search block written a
  session early, and [[Random Numbers]], [[Simulation]], and [[Neural Network]] all feed in.
- [[STATISTICS]] (MATH 2234): [[Probability]], [[Random Variable]], [[Conditional Probability]],
  [[Bayes Theorem]], [[Mean]], and [[Variance]] are the whole of block 2's machinery and half of
  blocks 3 and 4's.
- [[INFORMATION STRUCTURES]] (COMP 2631): [[Heap]] is the frontier, [[Graph]] and
  [[Weighted Graph]] are what gets searched, [[Tree]] is what a decision tree is, and
  [[Time Complexity]] is why heuristics exist.
- [[ALGORITHMS AND COMPLEXITY]]: owns the graph context around [[Dijkstra's Algorithm]], whose
  implementation note lives in `Leetcode/`. $A^*$ with $h = 0$ *is* Dijkstra, so the two sets of
  notes are describing one algorithm from two ends.
- [[INTRODUCTION TO COMPUTABILITY]] (COMP 2613): [[NP-Complete]] is why exact answers are
  unavailable, [[Turing Machine]] and [[Undecidability]] are the ceiling on any agent whatsoever,
  and [[Nondeterminism]] is the search-tree idea in its formal setting.
- [[LINEAR ALGEBRA FOR DATA SCIENCE]] (MATH 2303): [[Principal Component Analysis]] and
  [[Vector Norm]] are what clustering runs on.
- [[CALCULUS 1]] and [[MATHEMATICAL METHODS]]: [[Optimization]] and
  [[Multivariable Optimization]] are the gradient-based half that [[Genetic Algorithm]] is the
  alternative to.
- [[Systems of Logic]] in `Books/` is the classical-AI half this syllabus does **not** cover:
  knowledge representation, logical agents, and inference. Logged as a content gap, not written.
